analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 14 senators signed on, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently forbids Medicare from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill would repeal that ban and require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, including discounts and rebates, for drugs covered under Medicare's prescription drug benefit, with reports to Congress on the savings achieved.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly the tens of millions of seniors and disabled Americans enrolled in the prescription drug benefit, who would pay lower out-of-pocket drug costs if negotiated prices flowed into the program. Taxpayers also benefit because Medicare covers a large share of drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the current-law 'non-interference' provision that prohibits the Secretary from negotiating Part D drug prices, and replaces it with a requirement to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with manufacturers.
Applies to drugs covered under both standalone prescription drug plans and Medicare Advantage plans with drug coverage, so the benefit reaches the full Medicare drug program.
Requires semi-annual reports to Congress on the negotiations and the price discounts achieved, creating public accountability for the results.
Bars the Secretary from imposing a particular formulary and allows plans to negotiate even deeper discounts than the Secretary obtains, so plan choice and access protections remain in place.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenues would fall if Medicare negotiated lower prices on the drugs that account for a large share of federal drug spending. Some critics argue reduced revenues could modestly slow investment in new drug development.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the Secretary to negotiate but provides no penalty if a manufacturer refuses to reach a deal — no excise tax, no compulsory licensing, and no fallback price — so negotiators would lack legal leverage, unlike later versions of drug negotiation legislation.

Lower drug revenues are the industry's main counterargument: opponents contend that reduced manufacturer profits would mean somewhat less funding for research into new medicines, though the size of that effect is disputed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: Medicare is one of the biggest drug purchasers in the world, and negotiated prices would lower costs for beneficiaries and taxpayers. The main design weakness is that the bill offers no enforcement mechanism if manufacturers refuse to negotiate, so the projected savings depend on companies choosing to bargain. On balance it is a real but modestly engineered step that never got the chance to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 5, 2017, joined by eight original cosponsors including Democrats and Independent Sen. Angus King.
Thirteen additional senators cosponsored the bill — twelve Democrats and one Independent; no Republican signed on.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, whose jurisdiction covers Medicare; that was the bill's last action of record.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, with the Finance Committee never having held a markup or vote on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: the existing ban on Medicare price negotiation stayed in place for the full two-year Congress, and Medicare kept paying un-negotiated prices. Part D plan sponsors also avoided nothing but lost nothing, since the change never took effect.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it through introduction and referral.

for.name: 13 cosponsors (12 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Blumenthal, Shaheen, Baldwin, King, Brown, Leahy, Franken, and Kaine.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over Medicare
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their lobby
against.role: Industry sector affected by the bill
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory Medicare price negotiation, the policy the bill would enact.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to negotiate Medicare drug prices, including discounts and rebates, cutting into prices they currently set without negotiation. Their gain from the status quo is ordinary beneficiaries' cost.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and insurers
industries.note: Negotiated prices apply to what plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage organizations pay for covered drugs, so lower negotiated prices would reduce their drug costs while beneficiaries also save.

The bill preserves plans' ability to extract discounts below the negotiated price, keeping PBMs' negotiating role intact, but lower baseline manufacturer prices would shrink the margin between list and net prices they help capture.
